prompt: A yellow EXIT ONLY panel appears on the overhead sign above the lane you are driving in. What does it mean?
choices: Traffic entering from the ramp must leave at the next exit
The exit ahead is closed, so continue in this lane
Stay in that lane only if you plan to take the exit
Only trucks and buses may leave the highway here
explanation: An EXIT ONLY panel means the lane under it does not continue through the interchange; it becomes the exit ramp. If you want to stay on the highway, move out of that lane early.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.23)

prompt: Why is the road condition this sign warns about dangerous?
choices: Dropping a wheel off the edge can cost you control
The shoulder ahead is open only to emergency vehicles
The pavement ahead turns slick whenever it rains
The road narrows to one lane shared by both directions
explanation: This sign warns that the shoulder is lower than the pavement. If a wheel drops off, do not brake hard or jerk the wheel back; ease off the gas and steer back gently when it is safe, or you could lose control.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.20, FL p.58)

prompt: You are turning left on a green arrow. The arrow goes off and only a circular green light remains. What may you do?
choices: Keep turning without yielding, since your light is still green
Go straight only, because left turns ended with the arrow
Stop and wait for the arrow to light up again
Turn left after yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians
explanation: When the green arrow changes to a circular green, you may still turn, but the turn is no longer protected: oncoming traffic may now have a green light. Yield to oncoming vehicles and pedestrians first.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.11, NC p.82)

prompt: In a work zone, a large flashing arrow board shows a flashing bar or flashing corner lights instead of an arrow. What does it mean?
choices: Your lane is closed, so merge left right away
Work is going on near the travel lane, so drive with extra caution
The board is broken, so you can ignore it
All traffic must stop until a flagger waves you on
explanation: An arrow on the board tells you to move or merge in that direction. A bar or flashing corners (caution mode) means there is work beside the travel lanes ahead, with no merge required, so slow down and stay alert.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.23, IL p.76)

prompt: On a two-lane road with a double solid yellow center line, you want to turn left into a driveway. What is true?
choices: You must drive past and turn around, since the lines may never be crossed
You may cross them only if no traffic is in sight for a mile
You may cross the lines to make the turn when it is safe
You may cross them only during daylight hours
explanation: Solid yellow center lines mean no passing, but you may cross them to turn left into or out of a driveway, alley or private road when it is safe.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.26, CA p.19)

prompt: When are teen drivers statistically more likely to crash?
choices: When they carry other teens as passengers
When they drive alone
When a licensed adult rides in the front passenger seat
When a parent is supervising
explanation: Teen drivers with teen passengers are more likely to crash than when they drive alone or with adult passengers, because friends can distract them and encourage risk-taking. That is one reason many states limit teen passengers.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.36)

prompt: How does smoking while driving affect safety?
choices: It is not a distraction, because it does not involve a phone or a screen
It helps you stay alert on long trips
It only matters when the windows are closed
It is a distraction that can take your eyes and hands off driving
explanation: Lighting, holding and putting out a cigarette are distractions: they can take your hands off the wheel, your eyes off the road and your attention off driving.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.36, TX p.60)

prompt: You must slow down where drivers behind you may not expect it, such as just before a hidden driveway. How can you warn them early?
choices: Switch your headlights to high beam
Tap your brake pedal lightly a few times
Honk twice before you brake
Brake hard so they notice your lights sooner
explanation: Lightly tapping the brake pedal a few times flashes your brake lights and warns drivers behind you that you are about to slow or stop. Sudden hard braking invites a rear-end crash.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.48, CA p.18)

prompt: What is the best way to see what is behind you while you back up?
choices: Watch only the backup camera screen
Use only your side mirrors
Turn your head and look back through the rear window
Open your door and lean out to look back
explanation: Mirrors and cameras leave blind spots. Check behind the vehicle before you get in, then turn your head and look through the rear window while you back up slowly.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.42, NY p.42)

prompt: Why do driving handbooks stress letting other road users know where you are and what you plan to do?
choices: It gives you the right-of-way over them
It lets you skip checking your mirrors
It matters only on highways
It helps them predict your moves, which helps prevent crashes
explanation: Using your turn signals, brake lights, headlights and, when needed, your horn lets others see you and react in time. Signaling does not give you the right-of-way.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.48, CA p.17)

prompt: Your car's turn signals stop working during a trip. How should you signal turns until they are fixed?
choices: Use arm and hand signals out the driver's window
Flash your headlights before each turn
Turn on your hazard flashers each time you are about to turn
Tap the horn once for left and twice for right
explanation: If your turn signals fail, use hand signals: left arm straight out for a left turn, forearm pointing up for a right turn, and forearm pointing down to slow or stop.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.48, TX p.44)

prompt: In which of these situations is it most appropriate to sound your horn?
choices: You are passing a bicyclist on a narrow road
A child near the curb is about to run into the street
The driver ahead is slow to finish a turn
You are parallel parking and want others to wait
explanation: Use your horn when a crash is possible and someone may not see you, such as a child starting to run into the street. Do not honk at bicyclists or to hurry or scold other drivers.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.48, CA p.17, OH p.8)

prompt: Your car slides on ice and you cannot stop it from heading toward people at a bus stop. Besides working to regain control, what should you do?
choices: Flash your high beams at them
Turn on your hazard flashers only
Sound your horn to warn them
Turn the engine off right away
explanation: If you lose control of your vehicle, sound your horn to alert people nearby while you keep steering and braking to regain control.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.48)

prompt: What do your brake lights tell drivers behind you?
choices: That you are about to change lanes
That you are slowing down or stopping
That your parking brake is set and the car is parked
That you are about to turn
explanation: Brake lights come on when you press the brake pedal, warning drivers behind you that you are slowing or stopping. Turn signals, not brake lights, show turns and lane changes.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.48)

prompt: A driver backing out of a driveway is about to back into the side of your moving car and does not seem to see you. What should you do?
choices: Sound your horn to warn the driver
Flash your headlights at the driver
Wave your arm out the window
Turn on your hazard flashers
explanation: Your horn gets attention instantly. Use it when you think another vehicle is about to hit you, and be ready to brake or steer away.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.48, CA p.17)

prompt: How does driving after going without enough sleep compare with driving after drinking alcohol?
choices: Being tired affects only your eyesight, not your judgment
It is much safer, because tiredness fades once you start driving
Tiredness has no effect if you drink coffee first
The effects are similar: slower reactions and poorer judgment
explanation: Fatigue impairs driving much like alcohol. Being awake for about 18 hours affects driving about as much as a .05 BAC, and 24 hours about as much as .10. Only sleep cures drowsiness.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.37, FL p.43)

prompt: What are the main causes of deadly crashes in highway work zones?
choices: Wet paint and loose gravel
Workers stepping into traffic
Speeding and careless driving
Construction equipment breaking down
explanation: Carelessness and speeding are the main causes of work zone fatalities. Slow down, stay alert, obey work zone signs and leave extra following distance.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.58)

prompt: On a road with one lane in each direction, when may you pass the vehicle ahead on its right?
choices: Whenever it is going below the speed limit
When it is turning left and you can pass safely
When it is a large truck climbing a hill
Never, under any circumstances
explanation: Passing on the right is allowed only in limited cases, such as when the vehicle ahead is making or about to make a left turn, and only when you can do it safely.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.51)

prompt: You are in the center lane at an intersection, and the arrow painted in your lane points both straight ahead and to the left. What may you do?
choices: Go straight or turn left
Turn left only
Go straight only
Go straight, turn left or turn right
explanation: Lane-use arrows show the moves allowed from each lane. A combined straight-and-left arrow means you may go straight or turn left from that lane, but not turn right.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.53)

prompt: You are stopping behind another car on a steep uphill street. Why should you leave extra space in front of you?
choices: Your brakes work poorly when you face uphill
Drivers behind you need room to see the traffic light
It keeps your engine from overheating
The car ahead may roll back when it starts to move
explanation: On an upgrade, the vehicle ahead may roll backward as it starts to move, so leave a larger space cushion when you stop behind it.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.40, FL p.69)

prompt: What should you do with your speed when you make a turn?
choices: Keep the speed you had before the turn
Speed up to clear the intersection faster
Reduce it so you stay in control and in your lane
Brake hard in the middle of the turn
explanation: Speed is the most important factor in a turn. Slow down to a speed that lets you control the car, stay in your lane and react to pedestrians and other traffic.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.49)

prompt: The amount of space you need to cross or turn across traffic safely depends on what?
choices: Only whether you used your turn signal
The road, the weather and the oncoming traffic
Only how many cars are waiting behind you
Whether you have a stop sign or a yield sign
explanation: Whenever you cross traffic, you need enough space to do it safely. How much depends on road and weather conditions and on the speed and distance of oncoming traffic.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.50)

prompt: Which single action does the most to lower your risk of being hurt or killed in a crash?
choices: Driving only on weekdays
Staying in the right lane on highways
Keeping your headlights on during the day
Wearing your seat belt
explanation: Buckling up is the single most effective thing you can do to reduce your risk of death or injury in a crash. Air bags are designed to work together with seat belts.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.35, MI p.39, WA p.52)

prompt: The road is slick from rain or snow. How should you take turns and curves?
choices: More slowly than you would on a dry road
At your normal speed, braking hard in the middle
Faster, so you spend less time on the slick surface
At the same speed, but with your hazard flashers on
explanation: On slippery roads your tires have less grip. Slow down before turns and curves and take them slowly; hard braking or sharp steering mid-turn can start a skid.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.19)

prompt: Which of these is a distraction that raises your crash risk while driving?
choices: Checking your mirrors every few seconds
Scanning the road far ahead
Changing songs or adjusting the radio
Keeping both hands on the wheel
explanation: Adjusting a radio, music player or other audio device takes your eyes, hands and attention away from driving, just like using a phone. Set it before you drive or let a passenger do it.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.36, TX p.60)

prompt: In every U.S. state, what is the minimum age to legally buy alcohol?
explanation: All 50 states and DC set 21 as the minimum legal age to buy alcohol. Drivers under 21 also face stricter (zero tolerance) drinking-and-driving limits.
ref: State driver handbooks (e.g. PA p.88, NC p.35)
